opening.headline: When transitioning from an older model to a new one, we explore a procedure to safely handle the issue of agent behavior changes through evaluation and staged reflection.
body: The running agent is a prompt and tool configuration fine-tuned specifically for a certain model. When the provider notifies users of the model's discontinuation and recommends a replacement model, the tool invocation patterns or response formats may change for the same input, and some request patterns may result in errors with the new model.

In this class, we first review the model's lifecycle and observation period. Then, we examine code changes as specified in the migration documentation on a line-by-line basis, and proceed step by step to verify the process of gradually applying the model to a portion of traffic, with the ability to roll back if issues arise.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: This describes the impact of model support termination on the agent.
It is possible to determine the procedure of gradually incorporating a model that has passed evaluation.

screens.title: Concerned that the behavior might change when the Dawson model is discontinued
screens.lead: First, let's examine the situation of the team that received notice of model support termination. Read the following scene and consider what risks might be present.

visual.alt: A scene where a team that received notice of support termination compares different tool calling sequences produced by the same input, switching between the original model and the replacement model.
labels: We recommend using a substitute model.
List view → Order view → Order view → Summary

paragraphs: The running agent is a long-optimized result of prompt and tool configuration tailored to a specific model. However, the provider now notifies of the model's deprecation and recommends a replacement model. If not migrated, requests will eventually fail, making migration not a choice but a necessity.

The concern is that the behavior of the model may change. A replacement model might exhibit different tool-calling patterns or different response formats even with the same input. Some request patterns may even result in errors when using a new model. Users will first encounter these changes simply by renaming and deploying the model.
The question to be answered in this class is this: What procedure can safely reflect a model swap?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is model replacement simply changing one configuration value, or is it releasing a new version? I'll return to this question when the lesson ends.

screens.outro: First, let's recall our experience of switching models last time.

screens.title: What verification is performed before model replacement?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: When you switched models last time, what did you verify and what did you change?
items.answer: If you've directly tried a few requests and found them satisfactory, the verification scope remains limited to scenarios that come to mind manually. If an evaluation set is available, you can compare the existing model against the new model under the same criteria, making the assessment far more reliable than visual inspection alone.

items.prompt: Can you revert back to the original model if problems arise after making changes?
items.answer: Users continue to suffer damage whenever an issue occurs during the repair process if there is no rollback path. Separating the model name and request settings into distinct configuration values makes rollback easier. However, it's important to also understand that there will come a point when rollback is no longer possible for models that are no longer supported.

items.prompt: Do you know at a glance which model my service is using?
items.answer: If a model is dispersed across multiple services and API keys, it takes time to determine the scope of impact when a shutdown notice is issued. One method involves exporting usage by key and by model, which is covered in this course.

screens.outro: I've organized my thoughts now, so I'll check the model's lifecycle and notice period first.

screens.title: Model Support Ended: Lifecycle and Notification
screens.lead: The following flashcard explains the four stages of the model lifecycle and the notice period. Select a card to flip it over. To proceed to the next card, select the right-arrow.

visual.alt: Collection of stage icons to be placed on the front side of the card: green circle, gray circle, orange triangle, red rectangle.

cards.back: Active indicates that the model is sufficiently supported and is recommended for use. Legacy indicates that no further updates will be received and that it may be subject to discontinuation in the future. The Legacy designation should be interpreted as a signal to begin preparing to migrate to a new model.

Although it is still functional, it is no longer recommended. The provider will guide users to an alternative model and set an end date. This is when migration should begin. All usage must be migrated to the alternative model before the end date.

It is now in a non-operational state. Requests sent to a terminated model fail. Due to the time required for evaluation and staged rollout, it is safe to complete the replacement well before this state is reached.

Anthropic commits to providing at least 60 days of notice before terminating publicly available models and informs customers with active deployments. OpenAI states that it provides at least six months for general-purpose models and at least three months for specialized variants, while preview models may have as short as two weeks. The notice period varies depending on the provider and model type.

Google distinguishes between deprecation, which notifies of support discontinuation, and shutdown, which completely removes a model, and manages end-of-life schedules in a table format. Some models are not discontinued and automatically redirect requests to a new model. End-of-life schedules should be verified based on dates provided by the provider.

OpenAI provides the shutdown_date field in the models list API (GET /v1/models) so that the shutdown date can be programmatically verified. If the value is absent, it is null. Checking the shutdown date of the model being used in code can help prevent missing announcements.

screens.outro: Now that I understand the lifecycle, I'll review the code to see what has changed when migrating to the new model.

screens.title: Understanding the Impact Scope and Reading Migration Code Changes
screens.lead: The following summarizes the code changes indicated in the migration document, presented in hypothetical code form. You can view what the issue is and how to fix it by selecting the highlighted sections.

marks.note: This is code that assumes the first block is always text. In a thinking-enabled model, responses may begin with a thinking block, resulting in no text in the first block, and in such cases, some responses fail.

This is a form where blocks are read by type rather than position. Since only text blocks are selected regardless of whether "thinking" blocks come before or not, the response structure may vary depending on the model without causing any issues.

An option to force the invocation of a specific tool. According to the migration documentation, Claude Sonnet 5.5 returns a 400 error when forced tool selection is attempted. Instead, switch to guiding tool usage through instructions without relying on the option.

This is a prefill that pre-populates the last message with the assistant role. This approach also results in a 400 error when using the same model. To align the output format, alternative methods such as instructions or structured output must be used instead.

screens.outro: Having learned of the code change, I will outline the process of evaluating and gradually implementing it.

screens.title: Flow from evaluation through phased deployment and rollback
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to confirm the five-step process for safely reflecting a new model.

visual.alt: Evaluation gate, some traffic rollout, full expansion ongoing, with rollback to baseline if thresholds are exceeded.
labels: Evaluation Gate: Passed based on evaluation set criteria
Some traffic applications (e.g., a small percentage ratio)
Rollback: Return to previous model settings

steps.title: 1. Evaluation Gate
steps.body: Evaluate the benchmark set with the new model to verify that it passes the criteria. If it fails, it does not proceed to the next stage. The evaluation gate makes judgments based on predefined criteria, not human impressions, and records the results of the previous model as a baseline for easy comparison.

steps.title: 2. Applied to some traffic
steps.body: Upon passage, applies the new model only to a subset of traffic and monitors operational traces. Real inputs not present in the evaluation set may be introduced, allowing detection of issues missed during evaluation when the impact is minimal.

steps.title: 3. Ratio Expansion
steps.body: If the metric is maintained, the ratio is increased and the scope is expanded. At each expansion stage, costs, number of tool calls, and metric breakdowns by failure type are examined together. The impact when issues occur is smaller compared to changing the entire system at once.

steps.title: 4. If standards are violated, perform rollback
steps.body: If the metric exceeds the baseline, it is immediately reverted to the previous model configuration. For reversion to be easy, the model name and request settings must be separated from the code and defined within the configuration. Since it is assumed that the previous model has not yet terminated, action must be taken promptly before termination occurs.

steps.title: 5. Add failure to evaluation set
steps.body: Failures that have become rollback reasons are added to the evaluation set and used in the next iteration. Evaluation must be designed to be repeatedly performed via trace grading or dataset execution, so the same procedure can be followed each time during iteration.

screens.outro: Now that I understand the procedure, I'll apply it to cases where the tool invocation pattern varies across models.

screens.title: Explanation: Cases where the tool-calling pattern differs across models
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: After switching to a new model for the virtual support agent, some requests fail. The fact that only some requests fail, rather than all of them, is the clue. If the names were incorrect or the keys were wrong, all requests would have failed.

steps.title: Step 1: Observe using the evaluation set
steps.body: When we run the evaluation set, only some scenarios fail while the rest pass. The evaluation gate has filtered out issues before staged deployment. Open the trace of the failing scenarios to identify where the first discrepancy occurs.

steps.title: Step 2: Read one line of code
steps.body: The cause is one line: text = response.content[0].text. The new model has thinking enabled by default, so responses sometimes start with a thinking block, in which case there is no text in the first block. In some responses, text comes first and thus passes successfully, which is why only some cases failed.

steps.title: Step 3: Read Request
steps.body: When using forced tool requests, a 400 error occurs due to tool_choice. Instead of using forced call options, guide the model to use tools through instructions. This example demonstrates that the same tool-calling objective may be supported differently depending on the model's allowed request range.

steps.title: Step 4: Adjustment
steps.body: Modify the code to read blocks as type. In the tool usage loop, you must return the received thinking block unchanged, and since thinking uses max_tokens, you should also recheck that value. This adjustment is not merely a change in the model name, but rather a change in both code and configuration.

steps.title: Step 5: Reevaluation and Deployment
steps.body: Verify again that the entire evaluation set has passed, and then deploy a portion of the traffic. The failure types identified in this case are retained in the evaluation set. The same issue will be detected first in the next rollout.

screens.outro: Finally, I'll compile a checklist for verifying that the entire replacement is bundled into a single release.

screens.title: Explanation: Treat model replacement as a release
screens.lead: The table below summarizes model replacement as a timeline checklist. Review each row to verify what needs to be checked at each point in time.

data.caption: Model Swap Release Check List
rows: Understand the list of currently running models and their scheduled shutdowns, and read the migration documentation.
In the Console Usage Export section, verify the API key and model-specific usage, and check the expiration date through the provider's announcement and the model list API.
Records the baseline for the current model in the evaluation set.
A grader using the same evaluation set as the new model to benchmark its results
After passing the evaluation gate, apply it to some traffic.
Evaluation set pass/fail and operational trace
View cost, number of tool calls, and metrics by failure type together
Focusing solely on success rate overlooks efficiency degradation and new failure types.
Keep the rollback path and add the new failure to the evaluation set.
Increase in evaluation dataset for the next replacement and rollback records
data.notes: Model replacement is not simply changing a single configuration value; it is a release of a new version. Therefore, release safety mechanisms such as evaluation, phased rollout, and rollback are applied as originally designed. Even if the notice period feels long, considering the time required for evaluation and phased deployment, starting earlier provides more room to work with.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the contents so far.

screens.title: This is a model swap release.
screens.lead: Let's revisit the initial question by reflecting on the flow of the lesson.

paragraphs: End-of-support progresses according to the lifecycle and notice period, and replacement models may have different response formats and request options. Therefore, simply changing the name is not sufficient.

Once a model passes evaluation, deploy it to a subset of traffic and revert it if it deviates from the baseline. The answer to the initial question is to release a new version—i.e., a release. With a procedure that includes evaluation, staged deployment, and rollback, end-of-support becomes no longer a feared event but a planned operation.

glossary.def: This is the step where the provider notifies the user that model support has ended and provides information about the replacement model and the shutdown schedule.
This is a gate that new models must pass through evaluation criteria before proceeding to the next stage.
This is a rollout approach that starts with a portion of traffic and gradually expands based on metrics.
This refers to reverting to the previous model settings when the criteria are violated.
This document summarizes the code and configuration changes required when switching model series.

misconceptions.myth: A replacement model works exactly the same way just by changing its name.
misconceptions.fact: Code changes may be necessary depending on the response format or request options. The change log in the migration documentation should be reviewed.

misconceptions.myth: If the notice period is long, there's no need to rush.
misconceptions.fact: Evaluation and staged reflection take time. To allow sufficient notice period, initiation must occur early.

misconceptions.myth: Once replaced entirely, there is no need to revert.
misconceptions.fact: A rollback path should be maintained to handle cases that exceed the baseline.

misconceptions.myth: The first block of a response is always the response text.
misconceptions.fact: The new model can start with thinking blocks. Blocks must be read as types.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content covered in this course.
points: The model goes through a lifecycle from Active to Retired and is terminated after a notice period.
The new model may have different response formats and request options; refer to the migration guide.
Apply the approved model to a portion of traffic while maintaining a rollback path.
Since this is a model replacement release, it is managed using evaluation datasets and metrics.
closing.reflectionLead: Finally, here's a question for you to think about on your own. Please feel free to recall it at your convenience—no submission or grading is required.
closing.reflection: If the model currently being used by my agent expires tomorrow, what should I verify first, and in what order should I update to a new model?

title: Model end of support and gradual rollout

checks.q:
After switching to the new model, the following code fails only in some responses. The most likely cause is?  
text = response.content[0].text
options: Model name mismatch caused all requests to be rejected
The response starts with "thinking block," and the first block has no text.
Tool definitions are duplicated and the response is empty
checks.explain: A model with thinking enabled by default can start its response with a thinking block. The block must be verified as a type and the text block must be read.

wrong.0: If all requests are rejected, the symptom of only some responses failing does not match.
wrong.1: With that value, all requests would fail, which is different from the symptom where only some requests fail.
wrong.3: Duplicate definition provides no basis as a cause for this symptom.

checks.q: Try placing them in the order of gradually reflecting model changes.
items: Evaluate the dataset with the new model to verify that it passes the evaluation gate.
Apply the new model only to a portion of traffic and monitor operational traces.
If the indicator is maintained, increase the ratio and expand it overall.
If standards are violated, rollback to the previous model configuration and add the failure to the evaluation set.
checks.explain: First, pass through the evaluation gate, start with a subset of traffic and gradually expand, and revert if standards are exceeded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Consider that first it is filtered through the evaluation gate, then it starts in some part and expands from there.
